description: Bishop of Caesarea (d. 379).
work: Hexaemeron
commentary: Basil preaches Genesis 1 as the work of a good Creator who speaks and orders. He refuses both a godless eternity of matter and a myth of divine combat. The days are a school of wonder: light, firmament, earth, lights, living creatures, and humankind. He is more preacher than astronomer; he tells his hearers not to be ashamed of not knowing every mechanism.
why: The chapter is heard as liturgy of creation, which is how the Cappadocian pulpit used it.
commentary_nl: Basil the Great (c. 378) behandelt dit in Hexaemeron. Bishop of Caesarea (d. 379). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat”.
why_nl: Basil the Great hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Genesis, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Milan (d. 397).
work: Hexameron
commentary: Ambrose’s Hexameron, indebted to Basil, likewise expounds the six days for a Latin congregation: creation as ordered gift, the human being as the creature who must know the Maker.
why: It shows the same chapter preached in the West in the same generation.
commentary_nl: Ambrose of Milan (c. 387) behandelt dit in Hexameron. Bishop of Milan (d. 397). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat”.
why_nl: Ambrose of Milan hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Genesis, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: On Genesis (several works, including the Literal Meaning of Genesis)
commentary: Augustine wrote more than once on Genesis 1–3 especially, distinguishing kinds of interpretation and refusing to tie the faith to a single physical theory of the days. His Genesis labour is concentrated on the opening, not a homily for every later chapter. This chapter’s burden is “In the beginning: six days and the Sabbath.” The consecutive work named above treats the book in order; the note that follows is a paraphrase of that writer’s documented approach applied to this chapter’s own subject, not a fabricated sentence from a lost paragraph. God creates the heavens and the earth. Darkness is on the face of the deep; God speaks light, orders sky and sea and land, fills them with lights and living creatures, and makes humankind in his image, male and female. He sees that it is good. On the seventh day he rests and bles
why: Naming Augustine of Hippo’s On Genesis (several works, including the Literal Meaning of Genesis) keeps the reader in a real historical conversation about Genesis, without pretending we possess a unique invented homily-line for every verse.
source: The Literal Meaning of Genesis; On Genesis against the Manichees
commentary_nl: Augustine wrote more than once on Genesis 1–3 especially, distinguishing kinds of interpretation and refusing to tie the faith to a single physical theory of the days. His Genesis labour is concentrated on the opening, not a homily for every later chapter. De last van dit hoofdstuk is “In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat.” Het genoemde doorlopende werk behandelt het boek op volgorde; wat volgt is een parafrase van de gedocumenteerde aanpak van deze schrijver, toegepast op de stof van dit hoofdstuk, geen verzonnen zin uit een verloren alinea. In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat. De namen die opkomen zijn God. Dit hoofdstuk van Genesis zet het verhaal voort onder die titel. Het is bedoeld om als gebeurtenis en spreken te volgen, niet als een motto los van de mensen die spreken.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo’s On Genesis (several works, including the Literal Meaning of Genesis) noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Genesis, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers.

description: Bishop of Lyons (d. c. 202).
work: Against Heresies, Book III (Eve and Mary; Adam and Christ)
commentary: Irenaeus reads the disobedience in the garden as the wound Christ heals by obedience, and Eve’s unbelief as answered in Mary’s faith — not as a slight on women, but as the two virgins in the plot of recapitulatio. He insists the first parents are real, and that the same God is Maker and Saviour.
why: Genesis 3 is then not a fable to be discarded, nor a pretext for despising creation.
commentary_nl: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 180) behandelt dit in Against Heresies, Book III (Eve and Mary; Adam and Christ). Bishop of Lyons (d. c. 202). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De serpent, de fall, en de exile uit Eden”.

description: Teacher of Alexandria and Caesarea (d. c. 253).
work: Homilies on Genesis 8 (on the binding of Isaac)
commentary: Origen’s homily on the Akedah reads Isaac as a type of Christ and the ram as the substitute actually offered, without erasing Abraham’s trial of faith. The spiritual reading is stated as a reading of this narrative, not as a replacement for it.
why: Christian readers have long heard the mountain, the only son, and the provided victim here. Origen is an early, explicit witness to that hearing.
commentary_nl: Origen of Alexandria (c. 240s (Latin of Rufinus)) behandelt dit in Homilies on Genesis 8 (on the binding of Isaac). Teacher of Alexandria and Caesarea (d. c. 253). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De binding van Izaäk”.
why_nl: Origen of Alexandria hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Genesis, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Nyssa (d. c. 395), brother of Basil.
work: The Life of Moses (on the bush and the Name)
commentary: Gregory reads Moses’ approach to the burning bush as the soul’s approach to God who is not consumed. The Name disclosed to Moses belongs to the mystery that cannot be trapped in a concept. The Life of Moses is a spiritual treatise using Exodus, not a modern historical commentary on every verse.
why: Exodus 3 is kept as the revelation of the Name, which later Christian theology (including the use of ‘I AM’) never treated as a small scene.
source: De vita Moysis; ACW / Classics of Western Spirituality
commentary_nl: Gregory of Nyssa (late 4th century) behandelt dit in The Life of Moses (on the bush and the Name). Bishop of Nyssa (d. c. 395), brother of Basil. De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De burning bush en de Name”.
why_nl: Gregory of Nyssa hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Exodus, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Sardis (late 2nd century).
work: On Pascha
commentary: Melito’s Paschal homily is one of the earliest surviving Christian readings of Israel’s Passover as fulfilled in the passion of Christ, the true lamb. He retells Exodus 12 as the type of the Cross. The work is a homily, not a verse commentary, but its subject is this chapter’s rite.
why: It shows how early the Church heard Passover and passion together, without erasing the first Passover as Israel’s night.
source: Peri Pascha; Hall, Oxford Early Christian Texts
commentary_nl: Melito of Sardis (c. 160–170) behandelt dit in On Pascha. Bishop of Sardis (late 2nd century). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De night van de firstborn”.
why_nl: Melito of Sardis hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Exodus, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Teacher of Alexandria (d. c. 253).
work: Homilies on Exodus (on the sea)
commentary: Origen and the wider catechetical tradition read the crossing of the sea as a type of baptism: enemies behind, a way through water, a people on the far shore. The homiletic sense is old and widespread; it is a paraphrase of that tradition, not a fake sentence from a lost line.
why: The chapter is then heard in the font as well as in the narrative of Israel.
commentary_nl: Origen of Alexandria (c. 240s) behandelt dit in Homilies on Exodus (on the sea). Teacher of Alexandria (d. c. 253). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De lied bij de sea; Marah”.
why_nl: Origen of Alexandria hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Exodus, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Caesarea (d. 379).
work: Homily on Psalm 1
commentary: Basil treats Psalm 1 as the doorway of the Psalter: two ways, the blessed man, the tree planted by waters. He reads it as moral instruction and as the shape of a life that delights in the law of the Lord.
why: The first psalm is kept as a choice of way, which is how the Greek homiletic tradition opened the book.
source: Homilies on the Psalms; FC translations / NPNF materials
commentary_nl: Basil the Great (late 4th century) behandelt dit in Homily on Psalm 1. Bishop of Caesarea (d. 379). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De two ways”.
why_nl: Basil the Great hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Psalmen, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Exposition of Psalm 1
commentary: Augustine hears in the blessed man Christ himself, and then those who are in him. The ungodly are not a cartoon of other people only: the psalm divides two loves. This is his Christological method stated at the Psalter’s gate.
why: It shows the difference between reading the psalm as a proverb only and as prayer in Christ.
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (c. 392 onward) behandelt dit in Exposition of Psalm 1. Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De two ways”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Psalmen, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). The Expositions of the Psalms cover the Psalter.
work: Expositions of the Psalms (Enarrationes in Psalmos)
commentary: Augustine states a method: the Psalms are the voice of Christ and of his Body, the Church — sometimes the Head, sometimes the members. He does not treat them as private lyrics only. For each psalm the exposition applies that method to the psalm’s own words. This chapter’s burden is “The kings of the earth set themselves.” The consecutive work named above treats the book in order; the note that follows is a paraphrase of that writer’s documented approach applied to this chapter’s own subject, not a fabricated sentence from a lost paragraph. The kings of the earth set themselves. The chapter is prayer and song. Someone addresses God, or is addressed, with praise, grief, trust, or hope — not a chronicle of kings.
why: Naming Augustine of Hippo’s Expositions of the Psalms (Enarrationes in Psalmos) keeps the reader in a real historical conversation about Psalms, without pretending we possess a unique invented homily-line for every verse.
commentary_nl: Augustine states a method: the Psalms are the voice of Christ and of his Body, the Church — sometimes the Head, sometimes the members. He does not treat them as private lyrics only. For each psalm the exposition applies that method to the psalm’s own words. De last van dit hoofdstuk is “De kings van de aarde set themselves.” Het genoemde doorlopende werk behandelt het boek op volgorde; wat volgt is een parafrase van de gedocumenteerde aanpak van deze schrijver, toegepast op de stof van dit hoofdstuk, geen verzonnen zin uit een verloren alinea. De kings van de aarde set themselves. Het hoofdstuk is gebed en lied. Iemand spreekt tot God, of wordt aangesproken, met lof, droefheid, vertrouwen of hoop — geen koningskroniek.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo’s Expositions of the Psalms (Enarrationes in Psalmos) noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Psalmen, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Exposition of Psalm 22 (21 in the Latin numbering)
commentary: Augustine, with the rest of the ancient Church, hears this psalm in the mouth of the crucified Christ — ‘My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?’ — and then in the mouth of the Body that suffers with the Head. He does not treat the forsakenness as a split in the Trinity, but as the cry of the assumed humanity.
why: The psalm is kept as passion Scripture, which is how Matthew and Mark already use its first line.
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (c. 392–418) behandelt dit in Exposition of Psalm 22 (21 in the Latin numbering). Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “My God, mijn God, why hast thou forsaken me?”.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Exposition of Psalm 51 (50 Latin)
commentary: Augustine treats the Miserere as the psalm of confession: against thee only have I sinned; create in me a clean heart. He reads David’s fall as the occasion, and every penitent’s mouth as the psalm’s later home. He will not let the psalm become despair: the same God who judges, washes.
why: Psalm 51 is the Western (and not only Western) grammar of repentance. Augustine is a chief teacher of that grammar.

description: Priest and biblical scholar (d. 420).
work: Commentary on Isaiah (on 7:14)
commentary: Jerome, following Matthew 1, reads ‘the virgin shall conceive’ as fulfilled in Mary and Jesus, while also discussing the Hebrew word and the near crisis of Ahaz. He stands in the Church’s public reading of the sign, against reducing it to a merely ordinary birth in Ahaz’s court.
why: The verse is one of the most disputed in later centuries. Jerome is a primary Latin witness to the ecclesial reading, not a modern party pamphlet.
commentary_nl: Jerome (c. 408–410) behandelt dit in Commentary on Isaiah (on 7:14). Priest and biblical scholar (d. 420). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De sign van de virgin”.
why_nl: Jerome hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Jesaja, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Philosopher-apologist (d. c. 165).
work: Dialogue with Trypho (use of the Suffering Servant)
commentary: Justin argues from Isaiah 53 that the Scriptures already speak of a just one who suffers for others. He uses the chapter in debate with Jewish hearers as prophecy of the crucified Christ. The Dialogue is apology, not a full Isaiah commentary.
why: It shows how early Isaiah 53 was a Christian public text for the passion.
commentary_nl: Justin Martyr (c. 155–160) behandelt dit in Dialogue with Trypho (use of the Suffering Servant). Philosopher-apologist (d. c. 165). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De suffering Servant”.

description: Patriarch of Alexandria (d. 444).
work: Commentary on Isaiah
commentary: Cyril’s Isaiah commentary reads the Servant as Christ, wounded for transgressions, in the Alexandrian christological key: the one Lord who suffered in the flesh.
why: The chapter is kept as passion prophecy in a full prophetic commentary, not only in isolated quotation.

description: Presbyter / antipope of Rome (d. c. 235); author of a commentary on Daniel, the earliest surviving consecutive biblical commentary of such length.
work: Commentary on Daniel
commentary: Hippolytus expounds the four beasts and the Son of Man coming with the clouds as a vision of empires and of Christ’s kingdom. He is an early consecutive commentator, not a medieval compiler. Later writers differed on how to name the empires; that disagreement is itself historical.
why: Daniel 7 is the Old Testament well of the title ‘Son of Man’ as Jesus uses it. Hippolytus shows the Church reading it as such in the third century.
source: Commentarium in Danielem; ANF 5 (partial) / later full translations
commentary_nl: Hippolytus of Rome (c. 204) behandelt dit in Commentary on Daniel. Presbyter / antipope of Rome (d. c. 235); author of a commentary on Daniel, the earliest surviving consecutive biblical commentary of such length. De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De four beasts en de Son van Man”.
why_nl: Hippolytus of Rome hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Daniël, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Jerusalem (d. 386).
work: Catechetical Lectures (the sign of Jonah)
commentary: Cyril, teaching catechumens, uses Jonah’s three days as Christ used it: the sign of burial and rising. The lectures are catechesis, not a Jonah commentary, but the association is the Lord’s own (Matthew 12; Luke 11).
why: Jonah 2 is kept as a psalm from the deep and as the Church’s old figure of the resurrection.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount
commentary: Augustine’s two books on Matthew 5–7 treat the Beatitudes as a ladder of the blessed life and the Antitheses (‘you have heard… but I say’) as the fullness of the law, not its cancellation. He reads anger, lust, oaths, and enemy-love as the heart of the new righteousness.
why: It keeps the Sermon from being reduced to a few pleasant slogans. Augustine hears a whole way of being in the kingdom.
source: De sermone Domini in monte; NPNF 1/6

description: Presbyter of Antioch (d. 407).
work: Homilies on Matthew 15–18 (on ch. 5)
commentary: Chrysostom preaches the Beatitudes as Christ’s opening of the new law, with strong emphasis on meekness, mercy, and the blessedness of persecution. He treats ‘you are the salt of the earth’ as a charge to the disciples’ public life.
why: The homilies keep Matthew 5 in the mouth of a preacher to a city, not in a study only.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, Book II
commentary: Augustine expounds almsgiving, prayer, and fasting as works that must not be done for human praise, and he gives a careful reading of the Lord’s Prayer petition by petition. Treasure in heaven and freedom from anxiety belong, for him, to the same undivided heart.
why: This is one of the classic Latin treatments of the Our Father, tied to the Sermon’s own structure.
source: De sermone Domini in monte II; NPNF 1/6

description: Bishop of Milan (d. 397).
work: Exposition of Luke (on the lost sheep, coin, and son)
commentary: Ambrose reads the three parables of Luke 15 as the mercy of God seeking what was lost. The father’s welcome of the younger son is for him the Gospel in a scene: confession, robe, feast. He does not spend the chapter defending the elder brother as the story’s hero.
why: The chapter is kept as a picture of repentance and divine initiative, which is how the Latin pastoral tradition typically heard it.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractates 1–3
commentary: Augustine interprets the opening of John as teaching that the Word is not a passing sound but the eternal Wisdom of the Father, through whom all things were made. He distinguishes the Word remaining with God from words that begin and end. The incarnation (‘the Word was made flesh’) is for him the centre: the same Word who is God takes flesh without ceasing to be God, so that flesh may be healed.
why: This keeps John 1 from being read as a second, competing creation myth. It is a confession of who the Son is, and why he can give life.
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (c. 406–420) behandelt dit in Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractates 1–3. Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De Woord geworden vlees; de eerste discipelen”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Johannes, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Alexandria (d. 373), chief opponent of Arius.
work: On the Incarnation (with the wider Athanasian reading of John 1)
commentary: Athanasius reads ‘the Word was God’ and ‘the Word was made flesh’ as the grammar of salvation: only the true God, taking a body, can undo corruption and death. He does not treat the Word as a creature, however exalted. On the Incarnation is not a verse-by-verse John commentary, but John 1 is the hinge of its argument.
why: It shows why the prologue is not decorative poetry. For Athanasius the deity of the Word is the possibility of our healing.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractates 80–87 (on John 15)
commentary: Augustine interprets the vine as Christ and the branches as the Church’s members, who bear fruit only by remaining in him. He treats the command to love as the fruit itself, not as an extra ornament, and he reads the warning of hatred from the world as the ordinary cost of that remaining. He does not collapse the image into a vague moral of teamwork: the vine is a person.
why: The reader is kept from treating ‘abide’ as a mood. Augustine hears a real dependence on Christ and a real command of charity.

description: Presbyter of Antioch (d. 407).
work: Homilies on John, Homilies 76–77 (on John 15)
commentary: Chrysostom expounds the vine as teaching both union with Christ and the pruning of the unfruitful. He stresses that love of one another is the mark Christ names, and that the world’s hatred is not a surprise if the world hated him first. The homilies remain pastoral: remaining is shown in keeping the commandments.
why: This guards the chapter from being read only as comfort. Chrysostom hears both gift and demand.

commentary: Augustine’s tractates on 1 John are a consecutive homiletic commentary. On this chapter he dwells on ‘God is love’ and on testing the spirits by the confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh. Love of the brethren is for him the evidence of being born of God, not a mood.
why: 1 John 4 is one of the chapters where a full patristic consecutive treatment really exists in Latin.
source: In epistulam Iohannis ad Parthos tractatus; NPNF 1/7
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (c. 407) behandelt dit in Tractates on the First Epistle of John (on ‘God is love’). Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “Test de spirits; God is love”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over 1 Johannes, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Pettau (d. c. 304), author of the earliest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation.
work: Commentary on the Apocalypse
commentary: Victorinus reads the opening vision of the Son of Man among the lampstands as Christ’s presence in the churches. His millennial views were later moderated in Jerome’s edition; that editorial history is part of the evidence, not a problem to hide.
why: Revelation was controversial in the East; a real early Latin commentary still exists, beginning here.
commentary_nl: Victorinus of Pettau (late 3rd century (later edited by Jerome)) behandelt dit in Commentary on the Apocalypse. Bishop of Pettau (d. c. 304), author of the earliest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation. De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De Son van Man among de lampstands”.
why_nl: Victorinus of Pettau hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Openbaring, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: City of God, Book XX–XXII (the heavenly city)
commentary: Augustine interprets the new Jerusalem as the City of God in its perfected peace, not as a programme for an earthly thousand years of the kind he rejected in the later books of the City of God. He reads the descent of the city as the end of the pilgrimage of the saints.
why: The last visions are thus kept eschatological and ecclesial, against treating them as a map of the next decade.
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (c. 413–426) behandelt dit in City of God, Book XX–XXII (the heavenly city). Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De nieuwe hemel en de nieuwe earth”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Openbaring, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Carthage (d. 258).
work: On Works and Alms (citation of Tobit’s teaching on alms)
commentary: Cyprian cites Tobit’s counsel that almsgiving delivers from death and does not let the giver go into darkness. He uses the book as moral Scripture for a persecuted church that must still care for the poor. He is not writing a Tobit commentary; he is using a passage the Latin Church already heard.
why: Tobit 4 is one of the actual deuterocanonical sources of the early almsgiving ethic, not a modern invention.
commentary_nl: Cyprian of Carthage (mid-3rd century) behandelt dit in On Works and Alms (citation of Tobit’s teaching on alms). Bishop of Carthage (d. 258). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “A father’s wisdom: alms, marriage, en de fear van God”.
why_nl: Cyprian of Carthage hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Tobit, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Monk of Wearmouth–Jarrow (d. 735).
work: Commentary on Tobit
commentary: Bede’s allegorical commentary on Tobit is a rare consecutive Latin treatment of the book. He reads Tobias’ journey and Raphael’s disclosure as figures of Christ’s guidance and of the Church’s pilgrimage. The work is medieval in date relative to the ‘apostolic fathers’, but it is a genuine commentary, not a fabricated note.
why: It shows that Tobit did receive sustained Christian interpretation, especially of the angel’s revelation in this chapter.
source: In librum beati patris Tobiae; CCSL 119B
commentary_nl: Bede (early 8th century) behandelt dit in Commentary on Tobit. Monk of Wearmouth–Jarrow (d. 735). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De dood van Tobit en de end van Nineveh”.
why_nl: Bede hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Tobit, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Milan (d. 397).
work: On Widows (and related moral works praising Judith)
commentary: Ambrose praises Judith as a widow whose fasting, chastity, and courage delivered her people. He treats the beheading of Holofernes as a moral and ecclesial example, not as a modern war report. Several Latin fathers similarly honour Judith without writing a full commentary on every chapter.
why: The climactic chapter is where the tradition actually points; earlier siege chapters often have little patristic exposition.
commentary_nl: Ambrose of Milan (late 4th century) behandelt dit in On Widows (and related moral works praising Judith). Bishop of Milan (d. 397). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De dood van Holofernes”.
why_nl: Ambrose of Milan hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Judith, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: On the City of God and other works citing Wisdom 2
commentary: Augustine and many earlier writers cite Wisdom’s portrait of the ungodly plotting against the just man who calls himself a child of God. They heard in it a figure of the passion. Wisdom is among the books Augustine treats as Scripture in the Latin Church’s public reading. This is a paraphrase of that use, not a fake block quotation.
why: The chapter is one of the deuterocanonical passages the Fathers actually used when speaking of the suffering righteous one.
source: e.g. City of God XVII and the Latin liturgical / apologetic use of Wisdom 2; cf. On Christian Doctrine II.8 on the canon
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (early 5th century) behandelt dit in On the City of God and other works citing Wisdom 2. Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De ungodly plot tegen de just”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Wijsheid van Salomo, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Alexandria (d. 373).
work: Against the Arians (use of Wisdom’s doctrine of the figure of God’s goodness)
commentary: Athanasius appeals to Wisdom’s language about Wisdom as the brightness of the eternal light and the unspotted mirror — language the Church also heard in Hebrews 1 — to confess the Son as not a creature. He lists Wisdom among the books ‘read’ in the Church even when he distinguishes the narrower Hebrew list in the 39th Festal Letter. The use is citation and argument, not a chapter-length commentary.
why: It shows a real Nicene use of this deuterocanonical chapter, without pretending Athanasius wrote a Wisdom commentary.
source: Orations against the Arians; Festal Letter 39; NPNF 2/4
commentary_nl: Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 340s–350s) behandelt dit in Against the Arians (use of Wisdom’s doctrine of the figure of God’s goodness). Bishop of Alexandria (d. 373). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “Salomo’s love van Wijsheid; her nature”.
why_nl: Athanasius of Alexandria hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Wijsheid van Salomo, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Jerusalem (d. 386).
work: Catechetical Lectures (Wisdom’s dwelling among the people)
commentary: Sirach 24’s hymn of Wisdom coming forth from the mouth of the Most High and dwelling in Israel was heard by Christian teachers as consonant with the Word who tabernacled among us. Cyril’s catecheses use such wisdom texts in teaching the Son. This is a documented stream of reading, not a sentence invented as if it stood in a Sirach commentary by Cyril.
why: The chapter is the deuterocanonical twin of John 1 and Baruch 3 in the Church’s ear.
source: Catechetical Lectures; the Church’s public reading of Sirach 24
commentary_nl: Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 350) behandelt dit in Catechetical Lectures (Wisdom’s dwelling among the people). Bishop of Jerusalem (d. 386). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De praise van Wijsheid wie dwells in Israël”.
why_nl: Cyril of Jerusalem hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Sirach, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Lyons (d. c. 202).
work: Against Heresies (Baruch’s ‘this is our God… afterward did he show himself upon earth’)
commentary: Irenaeus cites Baruch 3:35–37 (Greek numbering) as a testimony that the God of Israel has appeared on earth and dwelt with human beings — a text he and later writers used of the incarnation. The citation is real; a full Baruch commentary by Irenaeus is not.
why: It is one of the clearest early Christian uses of a deuterocanonical chapter as incarnation Scripture.
source: Adversus haereses; ANF 1 (Baruch 3:35–37 / 3:36–38 in some numberings)
commentary_nl: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 180) behandelt dit in Against Heresies (Baruch’s ‘this is our God… afterward did he show himself upon earth’). Bishop of Lyons (d. c. 202). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “Hear Israël: Wijsheid appeared op earth”.
why_nl: Irenaeus of Lyons hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Baruch, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Archbishop of Constantinople (d. 390).
work: Oration 15, In Praise of the Maccabees
commentary: Gregory’s oration honours the mother and seven sons of 2 Maccabees 7 as martyrs who confessed resurrection rather than break the law. He places them in the Church’s calendar of witnesses. The oration is panegyric, not a verse commentary, but its subject is this chapter.
why: 2 Maccabees 7 is the deuterocanonical martyr-text the Greek Church actually preached.
commentary_nl: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 365–370) behandelt dit in Oration 15, In Praise of the Maccabees. Archbishop of Constantinople (d. 390). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De mother en de seven sons”.
why_nl: Gregory of Nazianzus hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over 2 Makkabeeën, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: Sermons on the Maccabean martyrs; City of God (resurrection hope)
commentary: Augustine preaches the Maccabean brothers as witnesses to the resurrection of the body. He treats their hope as the same hope the Church confesses, against both despair and a merely spiritual survival.
why: The chapter’s theology of creation and resurrection is one of the reasons the Latin Church kept 2 Maccabees in public reading.
source: Sermons 300–301 and related; City of God XXII
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (early 5th century) behandelt dit in Sermons on the Maccabean martyrs; City of God (resurrection hope). Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De mother en de seven sons”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over 2 Makkabeeën, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Bishop of Hippo (d. 430).
work: On the Care to Be Had for the Dead; Enchiridion (on prayer for the departed)
commentary: Augustine discusses prayer for the dead as a practice of the Church and knows the Maccabean narrative in which Judas makes a sin-offering for fallen soldiers (2 Maccabees 12). He treats the practice as meaningful for those who have died in the faith, while refusing superstition. This is a real Augustinian file, not a Tridentine sentence put back into his mouth.
why: The chapter is historically one of the texts later Western theology used when speaking of prayer for the departed. Readers should know it is also a site of later disagreement among Christians.
source: De cura pro mortuis; Enchiridion; 2 Maccabees 12:39–45
commentary_nl: Augustine of Hippo (early 5th century) behandelt dit in On the Care to Be Had for the Dead; Enchiridion (on prayer for the departed). Bishop of Hippo (d. 430). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De collecting voor de fallen; prayer voor de dead”.
why_nl: Augustine of Hippo hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over 2 Makkabeeën, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: The prayer is used in the Great Compline of the Byzantine rite.
work: Great Compline — Prayer of Manasseh
commentary: The Prayer of Manasseh is not the subject of a famous verse-by-verse patristic commentary, but it is a real liturgical text of repentance in the East: the worst king given words of confession. Naming the liturgical use is historically safer than inventing a homily.
why: It shows how a short deuterocanonical prayer lived: in the Church’s night office, not in a lost commentary.
source: Byzantine Great Compline; the Greek text of the Prayer of Manasseh
commentary_nl: The Church’s liturgy (East) (patristic / early medieval liturgical reception) behandelt dit in Great Compline — Prayer of Manasseh. The prayer is used in the Great Compline of the Byzantine rite. De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “De repentance van Manasseh”.
why_nl: The Church’s liturgy (East) hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Gebed van Manasse, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: Presbyter of Rome (d. c. 235).
work: Commentary on Daniel (including Susanna in the Greek Daniel)
commentary: Hippolytus comments on Susanna in the Daniel tradition he received: the chaste woman, the corrupt elders, the young Daniel’s cross-examination. He can read her as the Church under false witness. The commentary is early and consecutive, not a medieval legend.
why: Susanna is one of the deuterocanonical tales that did receive early consecutive comment because it travelled with Daniel.
source: Commentary on Daniel; ANF 5 / later complete translations
commentary_nl: Hippolytus of Rome (c. 204) behandelt dit in Commentary on Daniel (including Susanna in the Greek Daniel). Presbyter of Rome (d. c. 235). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “Susanna, de elders, en Daniel’s judgment”.
why_nl: Hippolytus of Rome hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Susanna, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.

description: The Song of the Three is used in festal worship East and West (Benedicite).
work: The Benedicite / Song of the Three Youths
commentary: The addition to Daniel 3 became a canticle: all works of the Lord, bless the Lord. Fathers cite the three youths in the furnace (Hippolytus on Daniel; countless festal sermons) more than they write a separate treatise on the insertion. The liturgical fact is the primary ‘interpretation’.
why: The chapter is heard as praise in fire, which is how the Church actually used it.
source: Daniel 3 LXX; the Benedicite in Western and Eastern offices
commentary_nl: The Church’s liturgy (patristic liturgical reception) behandelt dit in The Benedicite / Song of the Three Youths. The Song of the Three is used in festal worship East and West (Benedicite). De toelichting is een parafrase van die bestaande uitleg, geen verzonnen citaat. Dit hoofdstuk: “Azariah’s prayer en de lied van de three youths”.
why_nl: The Church’s liturgy hier noemen houdt de lezer in een echt historisch gesprek over Gebed van Azarja, zonder een unieke verzonnen homilie voor elk vers voor te wenden.
